rows.speaker: author

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The courtiers advise fighting magic with magic, but reject ordinary magicians as a risk of humiliation and defeat.
rows.anchor: it would not be appropriate to do this through ordinary magicians

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The assembly is scheduled for a festive day before noon in an accessible open field; people are urged to attend and support the magicians as protectors of the country.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The interrogative about assembling carries an exhortation to gather, an understated rhetorical style also found in earlier and later sūrahs.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The appeal is for everyone to want the magicians to win and to attend in support, since they are defending national honour.

rows.claim: These verses recount the magicians’ professional request for a reward and Pharaoh’s reply promising reward and favour if they prevail.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The preposition in the magicians’ oath carries the force of an oath; because Pharaoh was regarded as a deity, people swore by his honour when taking important steps.
rows.anchor: whenever people took an important step, they would swear by his honour

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wording shows that Moses’ staff exposed not only the magicians’ trick but also the nature of everything they had done; destroying their master trick revealed their skill’s frailty.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A magician with a spark of truth-seeking can best distinguish magic from miracle; the magicians therefore prostrate and confess faith in the Lord of the Worlds, Lord of Moses and Aaron, despite Pharaoh’s earlier anger at that title.
